issues.legal_issue: A complaint alleging a disputed sale arrangement and payment, without allegations supporting the criminal elements of the charged offences, does not disclose a prima facie criminal case.
material_facts: The complaint alleged an oral agreement to transfer a plot for an agreed price and payments toward that price.
It alleged that the sellers later denied receiving the payments and refused to transfer the plot.
The complaint placed the agreement in July 2002 but alleged that payments began in July 2000, making the account self-contradictory.
The complaint and recorded witness statements contained no allegations supporting criminal intent to deceive or other facts constituting the offences for which cognizance was taken.
issues.conclusion: The allegations, even if accepted as true, disclosed a civil dispute over a sale and did not make out a prima facie case for the charged criminal offences.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the material had to disclose allegations constituting the offences charged. It concluded that the allegations did not support the guilty intention or intention to deceive needed for the alleged cheating and did not otherwise disclose the charged offences under Sections 406, 419, 420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.complaint_concerns_sale_dispute: The complainant alleged an agreement to sell property and payments toward its price, followed by refusal to complete the transfer.
predicates.complaint_lacks_facts_supporting_crimina: The complainant's allegations and witness statements did not state facts supporting the criminal elements of the offences charged.
predicates.complaint_account_is_self_contradictory: The complainant alleged that payments began before the date on which the alleged sale agreement was made.

issues.definition: When a complaint describes a sale dispute, lacks facts supporting criminal offences, and contradicts itself on a material point, it does not disclose a prima facie criminal offence.

issues.legal_issue: The inherent jurisdiction to quash criminal proceedings should be exercised where the complaint discloses no offence and continuing the prosecution would be an abuse of process.
material_facts: The complainant challenged the refusal to quash a complaint and the cognizance taken on it.
The complaint and the statements recorded before cognizance disclosed no criminal offence, and the allegations amounted to civil liability between the parties.
The account of the agreement and payments was self-contradictory.
issues.conclusion: The proceedings presented an extreme exception warranting intervention; the refusal to quash was set aside, and the complaint, cognizance order and process were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, quashing is confined to extreme exceptions. As stated in Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal, the civil character of an act alone does not justify quashing if the act is an offence; however, the Court found that no offence was disclosed here and that the cognizance was an abuse of process. The Court also relied on Sections 406, 419, 420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code as the offences for which cognizance had been taken.

predicates.appeal_challenges_refusal_to_quash: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decision that refused to quash a criminal complaint or the process issued on it.
predicates.complaint_discloses_no_criminal_offence: The complaint, taken at face value, does not allege facts constituting a criminal offence.
predicates.continuation_would_abuse_process: The criminal proceeding rests on material that discloses only civil liability and does not support the offences charged.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges refusal to quash, the complaint discloses no criminal offence, and continuing the case would abuse process, the complaint and criminal process are quashed.
